<reason>B decisively distinguished enforceable, reciprocal safeguards from an Egyptian veto. A’s historical injustice and electricity-access arguments supported development, but not exclusive authority over shared drought risks. B directly answered the questions about standards and deadlock, while A rejected even independent, reciprocal constraints and offered no enforceable protection when interests conflict. A also repeatedly exaggerated safeguards into total power shutdowns, including misrepresenting B’s position in closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B used A’s rejection of any independently compelled slowdown to show that A opposed enforceability itself, not merely Egyptian domination. B then dismantled the claimed operational asymmetry: slowing additional storage need not stop generation, and predictable downstream restrictions can influence planting before shortages occur.</best_rebuttal>
